questions.q: Which range is reserved for IPv4 loopback?
questions.explain: 127.0.0.0/8 is loopback; 127.0.0.1 ('localhost') always refers to the local machine.

questions.q: A Windows PC shows the address 169.254.33.7. What most likely happened?
choices: It could not reach a DHCP server, so it self-assigned an APIPA (link-local) address
It received a public address from the ISP
questions.explain: 169.254.0.0/16 is APIPA/link-local. Hosts pick one when DHCP fails. Check the DHCP server, the cabling and any DHCP relay (ip helper-address).

questions.q: Why is a /30 a classic choice for a point-to-point WAN link?
choices: It has exactly 2 usable host addresses
It is the only prefix routers support
questions.explain: /30 = 4 addresses: network, 2 usable hosts, broadcast. Perfect for two routers. Many networks now also use /31 (RFC 3021) on point-to-point links.

questions.q: How long is an IPv6 address?
questions.explain: IPv6 addresses are 128 bits, written as eight groups of four hex digits separated by colons.

questions.q: What is the correct shortest form of 2001:0db8:0000:0000:0000:ff00:0042:8329?
questions.explain: Drop leading zeros in each group (0db8 → db8, 0042 → 42), then replace ONE run of all-zero groups with '::'.

questions.q: How many times can '::' appear in a single IPv6 address?
questions.explain: Only once. With two '::' the reader couldn't tell how many zero groups each one replaces.

questions.q: Which prefix identifies IPv6 link-local addresses?
questions.explain: FE80::/10 = link-local (every IPv6 interface has one; it's not routed). 2000::/3 = global unicast, FF00::/8 = multicast, FC00::/7 = unique local.

questions.q: Globally routable IPv6 unicast addresses currently come from which block?
questions.explain: Global unicast addresses (the IPv6 equivalent of public IPv4) start with binary 001, i.e. 2000::/3 (2000:: to 3FFF::).

questions.q: Which IPv4 address type does IPv6 NOT have?
questions.explain: IPv6 has no broadcast. It uses multicast instead, such as FF02::1 for all nodes on the link.

questions.q: In modified EUI-64, how is a 48-bit MAC turned into a 64-bit interface ID?
choices: Insert FFFE in the middle and flip the 7th bit of the first byte
questions.explain: Split the MAC in half, insert FF:FE, and invert the universal/local (7th) bit. For example, 00:1A:2B... becomes 021A:2BFF:FE...

questions.q: What is the IPv6 loopback address?
questions.explain: ::1 is loopback (like 127.0.0.1). '::' (all zeros) is the unspecified address.

questions.q: What is the default (classful) subnet mask for a Class C address?
questions.explain: Class A /8 (255.0.0.0), Class B /16 (255.255.0.0), Class C /24 (255.255.255.0). Modern networks use CIDR, but exams still ask!
Four contiguous /24s = 2² → borrow back 2 bits: /22. 192.168.0.0/22 covers 192.168.0.0–192.168.3.255.

questions.q: When designing a VLSM address plan, which subnets should you allocate first?
questions.explain: Allocate biggest to smallest so large blocks stay aligned on their boundaries and you don't fragment the space.

questions.q: The private block 172.16.0.0/12 ends at which address?
questions.explain: A /12 spans 16 second-octet values: 172.16.x.x through 172.31.x.x. 172.32.0.0 is public!

questions.q: Which block is reserved as 'shared address space' for carrier-grade NAT (CGNAT)?
questions.explain: RFC 6598 reserves 100.64.0.0/10 for ISPs' CGNAT. 192.0.2.0/24 is documentation (TEST-NET-1), 198.18.0.0/15 is benchmarking, 240.0.0.0/4 is reserved.

questions.q: How many bits are in an IPv4 address?
questions.explain: IPv4 = 32 bits (4 octets of 8 bits), giving about 4.3 billion addresses.

questions.q: How many bits are in an IPv6 address?
questions.explain: 128 bits: roughly 3.4 × 10^38 addresses. Enough for every grain of sand to have its own subnet.

questions.q: What prefix length is the standard size for an IPv6 LAN subnet (needed for SLAAC)?
questions.explain: IPv6 LANs are /64: 64 bits of network prefix plus a 64-bit interface ID. SLAAC requires a /64.

questions.q: Write the single summary route (network/prefix) for 10.1.0.0/24 through 10.1.7.0/24.
An IPv6 address that is delivered to the NEAREST of several devices sharing it is:
questions.explain: Anycast: several devices share one address and routing delivers to the closest one. Public DNS resolvers commonly use anycast.

questions.q: How can an IPv6 host configure its own global address with no DHCP server?
choices: SLAAC, using the prefix from Router Advertisements
questions.explain: With Stateless Address Autoconfiguration (SLAAC), the host learns the /64 prefix from a Router Advertisement and builds its own interface ID (EUI-64 or random).

questions.q: In IPv6, what replaces ARP?
choices: Neighbor Discovery Protocol (NDP, part of ICMPv6)
questions.explain: NDP uses ICMPv6 Neighbor Solicitation/Advertisement messages (sent to multicast, not broadcast) to resolve addresses.

questions.q: Order these prefixes from the LARGEST network (most addresses) to the SMALLEST.
questions.explain: The shorter the prefix, the more host bits and the bigger the network. /8 = 16.7 million addresses, /30 = 4.

questions.q: Order the steps of the 'magic number' method for finding a subnet's network address.
items: Find the interesting octet (where the mask isn't 255 or 0)
Block size = 256 − mask value in that octet
Find the largest multiple of the block size ≤ the IP's octet
That multiple is the network; next multiple − 1 is the broadcast
questions.explain: Example: 10.1.1.70/26 → interesting octet 4 (mask 192) → block 64 → 64 ≤ 70 → network 10.1.1.64, broadcast 10.1.1.127.

questions.q: You have one /24. Order these VLSM allocations the way you should assign them.
questions.explain: Biggest first: /25, then /26, then /28, then /30. Each block stays aligned and nothing overlaps.

questions.q: How many hexadecimal digits are in each group (hextet) of a full IPv6 address?
questions.explain: Each of the 8 groups is 16 bits = 4 hex digits (e.g. 2001:0db8:...).

questions.q: Host 10.0.13.200/21 must reach host 10.0.15.10/21 directly. Are they on the same subnet?
choices: Only if the mask is changed to /24
questions.explain: /21 → third-octet block size 8. 13 and 15 both fall in the 8–15 block, so both are in 10.0.8.0/21 (10.0.8.0–10.0.15.255).
